claim: Diarrhoea remains one of the leading causes of childhood mortality globally.
source: Diarrhoea remains one of the leading causes of childhood mortality globally.
evidence: This is a statement of established epidemiological fact about global childhood mortality.

claim: Recent epidemiological studies conducted in low-middle income countries (LMICs) identified Shigella spp. as the first and second most predominant agent of dysentery and moderate diarrhoea, respectively.
source: Recent epidemiological studies conducted in low-middle income countries (LMICs) identified Shigella spp. as the first and second most predominant agent of dysentery and moderate diarrhoea, respectively.
evidence: This claim references recent epidemiological studies, implying citation-based support.

claim: The rapid emergence of resistance against existing antimicrobials in Shigella spp. poses a serious global health problem.
source: The rapid emergence of resistance against existing antimicrobials in Shigella spp. poses a serious global health problem.
evidence: This is a statement drawing from established knowledge about antimicrobial resistance trends.

claim: Several known antimicrobial compound classes with antibacterial activity against Shigella were identified through high-throughput phenotypic screening.
source: We identified several known antimicrobial compound classes with antibacterial activity against Shigella.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental screening data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tebipenem was found to be highly potent against broadly susceptible Shigella and contemporary MDR variants.
source: These compounds included the oral carbapenem Tebipenem, which was found to be highly potent against broadly susceptible Shigella and contemporary MDR variants for which we perform detailed pre-clinical testing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental MIC data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tebipenem had activity against a wide range of other non-Shigella enteric bacteria.
source: Additional in vitro screening demonstrated that Tebipenem had activity against a wide range of other non-Shigella enteric bacteria.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro screening data against multiple enteric pathogens.

claim: Synergistic behaviour of two different drug combinations incorporating Tebipenem was identified.
source: Cognisant of the risk for the development of resistance against monotherapy, we identified synergistic behaviour of two different drug combinations incorporating Tebipenem.
evidence: This is supported by checkerboard titration assays and FIC calculations.

claim: The orally bioavailable prodrug Tebipenem pivoxil had ideal pharmacokinetic properties for treating enteric pathogens.
source: We found the orally bioavailable prodrug (Tebipenem pivoxil) had ideal pharmacokinetic properties for treating enteric pathogens and was effective in clearing the gut of infecting organisms when administered to Shigella-infected mice and gnotobiotic piglets.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacokinetic studies in mice and piglets presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tebipenem pivoxil was effective in clearing the gut of infecting organisms when administered to Shigella-infected mice and gnotobiotic piglets.
source: We found the orally bioavailable prodrug (Tebipenem pivoxil) had ideal pharmacokinetic properties for treating enteric pathogens and was effective in clearing the gut of infecting organisms when administered to Shigella-infected mice and gnotobiotic piglets.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo efficacy studies in animal models.

claim: Tebipenem pivoxil is licenced for paediatric respiratory tract infections in Japan.
source: Our data highlight the emerging antimicrobial resistance crisis and shows that Tebipenem pivoxil (licenced for paediatric respiratory tract infections in Japan) should be accelerated into human trials and could be repurposed as an effective treatment for severe diarrhoea caused by MDR Shigella and other enteric pathogens in LMICs.
evidence: This is a statement of regulatory fact about the drug's current licensure.

claim: Tebipenem pivoxil should be accelerated into human trials and could be repurposed as an effective treatment for severe diarrhoea caused by MDR Shigella and other enteric pathogens in LMICs.
source: Our data highlight the emerging antimicrobial resistance crisis and shows that Tebipenem pivoxil (licenced for paediatric respiratory tract infections in Japan) should be accelerated into human trials and could be repurposed as an effective treatment for severe diarrhoea caused by MDR Shigella and other enteric pathogens in LMICs.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental data presented and represents speculation about future clinical use.

claim: Humanity is currently in the midst of a global antimicrobial resistance (AMR) crisis.
source: Humanity is currently in the midst of a global antimicrobial resistance (AMR) crisis (Theuretzbacher, 2017; Antimicrobial Resistance Collaborators, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on AMR.

claim: Many antimicrobials have lost or are rapidly losing their efficacy against common bacterial pathogens.
source: Many of the antimicrobials that we rely on to treat and/or control infections caused by common bacterial pathogens have lost or are rapidly losing their efficacy.
evidence: This is a statement drawing from established knowledge about antimicrobial resistance trends.

claim: Diarrhoea accounts for approximately 1.3 million deaths globally annually, with the preponderance occurring in young children residing in LMICs.
source: Annually, diarrhoea accounts for approximately 1.3 million deaths globally, with the preponderance of these occurring in young children residing in LMICs (Kotloff, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published epidemiological data.

claim: Antimicrobials are a key tool in limiting the impact of enteric infections in LMICs due to a lack of other scalable approaches.
source: Due to a lack of other scalable approaches, antimicrobials are a key tool in limiting the impact of these infections, but the trajectory of AMR describes an escalating problem, especially in vulnerable populations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current state of public health interventions.

claim: Shigella are associated with ~125 million diarrhoeal episodes and 200,000 deaths annually.
source: Recent estimates suggest that Shigella are associated with ~125 million diarrhoeal episodes and 200,000 deaths annually (Khalil et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published epidemiological estimates.

claim: Shigella along with enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) were the most predominant bacterial pathogens in the stools of paediatric diarrhoeal patients in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa.
source: Additionally, Shigella along with enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC), were the most predominant bacterial pathogens in the stools of paediatric diarrhoeal patients in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa (Kotloff et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Shigella were the most prevalent pathogen in diarrhoeal children aged 2–5 years.
source: This study also found that Shigella were the most prevalent pathogen in diarrhoeal children aged 2–5 years; a reanalysis of stool samples from this study using more sensitive molecular approaches suggested that burden of Shigella may actual be double that of previous estimates (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The burden of Shigella may be double that of previous estimates based on reanalysis using more sensitive molecular approaches.
source: This study also found that Shigella were the most prevalent pathogen in diarrhoeal children aged 2–5 years; a reanalysis of stool samples from this study using more sensitive molecular approaches suggested that burden of Shigella may actual be double that of previous estimates (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published reanalysis study.

claim: Clinical evidence strongly supports the use of antimicrobials to treat severe Shigella associated diarrhoea.
source: Clinical evidence strongly supports the use of antimicrobials to treat severe Shigella associated diarrhoea (Kotloff et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published clinical evidence.

claim: Appropriate antimicrobial therapy reduces the duration of fever and diarrhoea associated with Shigella by 1–2 days.
source: Appropriate antimicrobial therapy reduces the duration of fever and diarrhoea associated with Shigella by 1–2 days, which in turn limits the severity of symptoms and the risk of further complications (Vinh et al., 2000; Christopher et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published clinical studies.

claim: Antimicrobial therapy limits the severity of symptoms and the risk of further complications in Shigella infections.
source: Appropriate antimicrobial therapy reduces the duration of fever and diarrhoea associated with Shigella by 1–2 days, which in turn limits the severity of symptoms and the risk of further complications (Vinh et al., 2000; Christopher et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduction in disease duration.

claim: The shedding of Shigella in the stools is restricted by antimicrobials, which reduces onward transmission.
source: Additionally, the shedding of the pathogen in the stools is restricted by antimicrobials, which then reduce onward transmission.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of antimicrobial action.

claim: There is currently no licenced vaccine for Shigella.
source: As there is currently no licenced vaccine for Shigella, antimicrobials are one of the only reliable mechanisms available for disease control (Levine et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement of regulatory fact supported by citation.

claim: Antimicrobials are one of the only reliable mechanisms available for Shigella disease control.
source: As there is currently no licenced vaccine for Shigella, antimicrobials are one of the only reliable mechanisms available for disease control (Levine et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of vaccines and the efficacy of antimicrobials.

claim: Shigella are highly adept at acquiring multi-drug resistance (MDR) plasmids from other members of the Enterobacteriaceae.
source: However, Shigella are highly adept at acquiring multi-drug resistance (MDR) plasmids from other member of the Enterobacteriaceae and resistance mutations are commonly associated with 'successful' lineages (Baker et al., 2015; Chung The et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on Shigella genetics.

claim: Resistance mutations are commonly associated with 'successful' Shigella lineages.
source: However, Shigella are highly adept at acquiring multi-drug resistance (MDR) plasmids from other member of the Enterobacteriaceae and resistance mutations are commonly associated with 'successful' lineages (Baker et al., 2015; Chung The et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on Shigella evolution.

claim: The WHO recommends ciprofloxacin, azithromycin, pivmecillinam, and ceftriaxone as the empirical drug choices for Shigella infections.
source: Consequently, there has been an 'arms race' between the pathogen and antimicrobials, with the WHO ultimately recommending ciprofloxacin, azithromycin, pivmecillinam, and ceftriaxone as the empirical drug choices for Shigella infections (Williams and Berkley, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to WHO guidelines.

claim: Resistance to ciprofloxacin, azithromycin, pivmecillinam, and ceftriaxone has emerged in Shigella.
source: Inevitably, resistance to these antimicrobials has emerged and increasingly resistant organisms, such as extensively drug resistant (XDR) Shigella sonnei in Vietnam (Thanh Duy et al., 2020), are spreading across LMICs (Chung The et al., 2019), in travellers returning from LMICs (Baker et al., 2016), and in men-who-have-sex-with-men (MSM) (Baker et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on antimicrobial resistance.

claim: Extensively drug resistant (XDR) Shigella sonnei are spreading across LMICs, in travellers returning from LMICs, and in men-who-have-sex-with-men (MSM).
source: Inevitably, resistance to these antimicrobials has emerged and increasingly resistant organisms, such as extensively drug resistant (XDR) Shigella sonnei in Vietnam (Thanh Duy et al., 2020), are spreading across LMICs (Chung The et al., 2019), in travellers returning from LMICs (Baker et al., 2016), and in men-who-have-sex-with-men (MSM) (Baker et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published epidemiological studies.

claim: The US-CDC has declared AMR Shigella a serious global health threat requiring new interventions.
source: Accordingly, the US-CDC has declared AMR Shigella a serious global health threat requiring new interventions and the WHO has placed them on the global priority list of antibiotic-resistant bacteria to guide research, discovery, and development of new antibiotics (The World Health Organisation, 2007).
evidence: This is a statement of public health policy supported by citation.

claim: The WHO has placed AMR Shigella on the global priority list of antibiotic-resistant bacteria to guide research, discovery, and development of new antibiotics.
source: Accordingly, the US-CDC has declared AMR Shigella a serious global health threat requiring new interventions and the WHO has placed them on the global priority list of antibiotic-resistant bacteria to guide research, discovery, and development of new antibiotics (The World Health Organisation, 2007).
evidence: This is a statement of public health policy supported by citation.

claim: Target-based drug discovery programmes after the genomics revolution of the 1990s produced largely disappointing results due to lack of translation from target-activity to whole-cell activity.
source: After the genomics revolution of the 1990s, the research community embarked on a series of target-based drug discovery programmes to identify novel antimicrobial compounds. This strategy, because of lack of translation from target-activity to whole-cell activity, produced largely disappointing results (Gwynn et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature on drug discovery.

claim: Phenotypic antimicrobial screens have proven to yield a higher hit rate than target-based approaches.
source: Conversely, phenotypic antimicrobial screens have proven to yield a higher hit rate than target-based approaches with several successful examples in infectious diseases (Gamo et al., 2010; Ballell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies on drug discovery methods.

claim: An academic-industrial collaboration was established to perform in vitro phenotypic screening of ~1.7 million compounds against antimicrobial susceptible and MDR Shigella.
source: Aiming to identify compounds with activity against MDR Shigella, we established an academic-industrial collaboration (Ballell et al., 2016), creating a platform to perform in vitro phenotypic screening of ~1.7 million compounds against antimicrobial susceptible and MDR Shigella.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: The compound collection screened comprised a combination of naive chemistry, compounds originating from previous antibacterial drug discovery programs, and currently marketed antimicrobials.
source: We interrogated a collection of compounds spanning broad chemical diversity, comprised of a combination of naive chemistry, compounds originating from previous antibacterial drug discovery programs, and currently marketed antimicrobials.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials used in the study.

claim: Several lead chemical classes with previously reported antimicrobial activity were identified through the screening approach.
source: Using this approach, we identified several lead chemical classes with previously reported antimicrobial activity, opting to further characterise Tebipenem (Yao et al., 2016), an oral carbapenem, that could be rapidly accelerated into clinical testing to treat infections caused by MDR Shigella and other gastrointestinal pathogens.
evidence: This is supported by the screening data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tebipenem is an oral carbapenem that could be rapidly accelerated into clinical testing to treat infections caused by MDR Shigella and other gastrointestinal pathogens.
source: Using this approach, we identified several lead chemical classes with previously reported antimicrobial activity, opting to further characterise Tebipenem (Yao et al., 2016), an oral carbapenem, that could be rapidly accelerated into clinical testing to treat infections caused by MDR Shigella and other gastrointestinal pathogens.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the experimental data and represents speculation about future clinical development.

claim: A high-throughput screening (HTS) method was developed to identify compounds that could inhibit the growth of Shigella flexneri 2457T in Müller Hinton medium.
source: We developed a high-throughput screening (HTS) method to identify compounds that could inhibit the growth of Shigella flexneri 2457T in Müller Hinton medium (Sigma Aldrich, UK).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method developed for the study.

claim: A resazurin reduction protocol was adapted as a surrogate readout for bacterial viability because it provided a stable signal, a low interference level, and was cost effective.
source: We adapted a resazurin reduction protocol from Franzblau et al. as surrogate readout for bacterial viability because it provided a stable signal, a low interference level, and was cost effective (Franzblau et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method with citation to the original protocol.

claim: The assay was performed in 1536-well polystyrene assay plates and used to screen ~1.7 million compounds.
source: The assay was performed in 1536-well polystyrene assay plates (HiBase, μClear, Greiner Bio‐One) and used to screen ~1.7 million compounds from (a) GSK naïve chemical diversity, (b) GSK antibacterial programs, and (c) marketed antimicrobial agents.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method and scale.

claim: The GSK compound screening set was sub-selected from the 8 million compound GSK collection using principles described by Harper and co-workers.
source: The GSK compound screening set was sub-selected from the 8 million compound GSK collection using the principles described by Harper and co-workers (Harper et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a description of the compound selection method with citation.

claim: The set of 4000 compounds with known antibacterial pedigree from the GSK antibacterial programs was selected using an MIC <1 µM against E. coli as cut-off value.
source: The set of 4000 compounds with known antibacterial pedigree from the GSK antibacterial programs was selected from GSK compound collection using an MIC <1 µM against E. coli as cut-off value for selection.
evidence: This is a description of the compound selection criteria.

claim: The set of marketed antibacterial agents included most commercial antimicrobial agents.
source: The set of marketed antibacterial agents included most commercial antimicrobial agents.
evidence: This is a description of the compound collection composition.

claim: The final assay volume was 5 μl and the final compound concentration was 10 µM.
source: The final assay volume was 5 μl and the final compound concentration was 10 µM.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions.

claim: A robust Z' mean value of 0.7 and a signal/noise ratio of 12 were obtained from the screening.
source: A mean OD with three standard deviations cut-off was used and a robust Z' mean value of 0.7 and a signal/noise ratio of 12 were obtained from the screening.
evidence: This is a report of the screening assay quality metrics.

claim: At an average statistical activity cut-off of 25.48%, 6970 primary hits were identified, representing an overall hit rate of 0.41%.
source: At an average statistical activity cut-off of 25.48%, 6970 primary hits were identified, representing an overall hit rate of 0.41%, which is lower than the typical hit rates for phenotypic high throughput screens (~1%).
evidence: This is a report of the screening results.

claim: The hit rate of 0.41% is lower than the typical hit rates for phenotypic high throughput screens (~1%).
source: At an average statistical activity cut-off of 25.48%, 6970 primary hits were identified, representing an overall hit rate of 0.41%, which is lower than the typical hit rates for phenotypic high throughput screens (~1%).
evidence: This is a comparison of the observed hit rate to typical rates, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: 4006 compounds fulfilled confirmation criteria and were progressed to dose response inhibition curves against Shigella 2457T.
source: Compounds fulfilling confirmation criteria (n = 4006) were progressed to dose response inhibition curves against Shigella 2457T, which were performed in duplicate.
evidence: This is a report of the screening progression results.

claim: 2269 compounds in seven classes inhibited the growth of Shigella flexneri 2457T with an IC50 ≤1 µM.
source: Ultimately, 2269 compounds in seven classes (bacterial topoisomerase inhibitors (BTIs), inhibitors of UDP-3-O-(R-3-hydroxymyristoyl)-N-acetylglucosamine deacetylase (LpxCs), microcin PDI, Met-tRNA inhibitors, β-lactams, fluoroquinolones, and pleuromutilins) were identified that inhibited the growth of Shigella flexneri 2457T with an IC50 ≤1 µM (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a report of the screening results with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: 297 compounds generated an MIC ≤10 µM against both S. flexneri EG478 and S. sonnei 02–1181.
source: From the 2269 compounds evaluated, 297 generated an MIC ≤10 µM against both organisms.
evidence: This is a report of the screening results against clinical isolates.

claim: The 297 compounds belonged to only three already known antibacterial classes: β-lactams, BTIs, and LpxCs.
source: The 297 compounds belonged to only three already known antibacterial classes: β-lactams, BTIs, and LpxCs.
evidence: This is a report of the chemical classification of the final hits.

claim: No hits representing new chemical diversity, NCEs, or compounds with novel modes of action were identified.
source: Notably, we did not identify any hits representing new chemical diversity, NCEs, or compounds with novel modes of action.
evidence: This is a report of the absence of novel compounds in the screening results.

claim: The majority of BTIs, LpxCs, and carbapenems had a notable loss of potency when tested against the two clinical MDR Shigella isolates in comparison to the original laboratory reference organism.
source: Additionally, the majority of BTIs, LpxCs, and carbapenems had a notable loss of potency when tested against the two clinical MDR Shigella isolates in comparison to the original laboratory reference organism (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a report of the comparative potency data with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The loss of potency against clinical isolates highlights the requirement for representative contemporary bacterial isolates for drug screening campaigns and the development of novel antimicrobials.
source: This trend highlights the requirement for representative contemporary bacterial isolates for drug screening campaigns and the development of novel antimicrobials.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed loss of potency.

claim: Meropenem, Tebipenem, and Ertapenem exhibited the greatest bactericidal activity against the two MDR Shigella clinical isolates.
source: Meropenem, Tebipenem, and Ertapenem were identified via the screening and exhibited the greatest bactericidal activity against the two MDR Shigella clinical isolates (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a report of the comparative activity data.

claim: Tebipenem pivoxil is administered orally, while Meropenem and Ertapenem are administered parenterally or intramuscularly.
source: Notably, Tebipenem pivoxil is administered orally, while Meropenem and Ertapenem are administered parenterally or intramuscularly.
evidence: This is a statement of known pharmacological properties of these drugs.

claim: Tebipenem pivoxil has good oral bioavailability and is commercially available in Japan.
source: Therefore, Tebipenem was of specific interest as the pivoxil prodrug has good oral bioavailability and is commercially available in Japan (Jain et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement of known pharmacological properties supported by citation.

claim: An oral drug with potential for accumulation in the gastrointestinal tract would be a suitable profile for treating invasive enteric pathogens.
source: We considered that an oral drug with potential for accumulation in the gastrointestinal tract would be a suitable profile for treating invasive enteric pathogens; therefore, we reasoned that Tebipenem may be the most appropriate identified compound that could be accelerated into further investigations for treating MDR/XDR Shigella infections.
evidence: This is a logical inference about desirable drug properties for enteric infections.

claim: Tebipenem inhibited the growth of S. flexneri 2457T with a potency comparable to current first line antimicrobials including ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone.
source: Using in vitro assays, we found that Tebipenem inhibited the growth of S. flexneri 2457T with a potency comparable to current first line antimicrobials in broadly susceptible organisms, including both ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data presented in Table 1.

claim: Tebipenem exhibited consistent in vitro activity against all clinical isolates of Shigella, with MIC values ranging from 0.04 to 0.3 µM.
source: The compound exhibited consistent in vitro activity against all clinical isolates of Shigella, with MIC values ranging from 0.04 to 0.3 µM (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Tebipenem generated substantially lower MICs than ciprofloxacin in isolates from Vietnam.
source: Particularly, Tebipenem generated substantially lower MICs than ciprofloxacin in isolates from Vietnam and had good in vitro activity against all MDR and XDR S. sonnei (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by comparative MIC data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Tebipenem had good in vitro activity against all MDR and XDR S. sonnei.
source: Particularly, Tebipenem generated substantially lower MICs than ciprofloxacin in isolates from Vietnam and had good in vitro activity against all MDR and XDR S. sonnei (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: Tebipenem retained good bactericidal activity against Salmonella, Campylobacter jejuni, and E. coli with a median MIC of <0.1 µM against all organisms.
source: Tebipenem retained good bactericidal activity against all three genera with a median MIC of <0.1 µM against all organisms (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data presented in Figure 2A.

claim: The frequency of spontaneous Tebipenem resistance mutations was calculated as <1.2 × 10–9, which is low and comparable to other currently available antimicrobials including fluoroquinolones.
source: The frequency of spontaneous resistance against Tebipenem was calculated as <1.2 × 10–9, which is low and was comparable to other currently available antimicrobials, including the fluroquinolones (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on spontaneous resistance frequency.

claim: Tebipenem had protracted antibacterial activity against Shigella at higher concentrations (2–4 x MIC).
source: The time kill experiments further demonstrated that Tebipenem had protracted antibacterial activity against Shigella at higher concentrations (2–4 x MIC).
evidence: This is supported by time-kill curve data.

claim: Population rebounds occurred at lower Tebipenem concentrations (0.5–1 x MIC) after 6 hr exposure in all three isolates.
source: Population rebounds occurred at lower concentrations (0.5–1 x MIC) after 6 hr exposure in all three isolates (Figure 2B, C and D).
evidence: This is supported by time-kill curve data presented in Figures 2B, C, and D.

claim: Tebipenem exhibited partial synergy in combination with the LpxC inhibitor, reducing the MIC against Tebipenem > 10 fold in S. flexneri, S. Typhimurium, and E. coli.
source: Tebipenem exhibited partial synergy in combination with the LpxC inhibitor, reducing the MIC against Tebipenem > 10 fold in all three organisms (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by synergy assay data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Tebipenem demonstrated partial synergy with azithromycin against S. flexneri and S. Typhimurium, but this combination appeared to show indifference or antagonism against E. coli.
source: Similarly, Tebipenem demonstrated partial synergy with azithromycin against S. flexneri and S. Typhimurium, but this combination appeared to show indifference or antagonism against E. coli.
evidence: This is supported by synergy assay data.

claim: In combination with ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone, and mecillinam, Tebipenem exhibited indifference or partial synergy against S. flexneri, S. Typhimurium, and E. coli.
source: In combination with ciprofloxacin, ceftriaxone, and mecillinam, Tebipenem exhibited indifference or partial synergy against all three organisms (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by synergy assay data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: The combination of Tebipenem/LpxC inhibitor exhibited indifference or partial synergy in vitro against all tested enteric pathogens (Salmonella spp., Shigella spp., K. pneumoniae, and E. coli).
source: The combination of Tebipenem/LpxC inhibitor exhibited indifference or partial synergy in vitro against all tested enteric pathogens (Salmonella spp., Shigella spp., K. pneumoniae, and E. coli).
evidence: This is supported by synergy assay data against clinical isolates.

claim: The combination of Tebipenem with azithromycin was particularly synergistic in vitro against a range of invasive and non-invasive Salmonella isolates, with FIC scores of ~0.5.
source: Notably, the combination of Tebipenem with azithromycin was particularly synergistic in vitro against a range of invasive and non-invasive Salmonella isolates, with FIC scores of ~0.5 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by synergy assay data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Tebipenem pivoxil is currently approved in Japan under the brand name Orapenem for the treatment of respiratory tract infections.
source: Tebipenem pivoxil, under the brand name Orapenem, is currently approved in Japan for the treatment of respiratory tract infections.
evidence: This is a statement of regulatory fact.

claim: The doses for pharmacokinetics and efficacy studies were extrapolated from the approved doses in children (4 and 6 mg/kg bid).
source: The doses for pharmacokinetics and efficacy studies were extrapolated from the approved doses in children (4 and 6 mg/kg bid) and we calculated equivalent doses in terms of systemic exposure in the animal species used for the efficacy and pharmacokinetic studies (described in Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the dose calculation method.

claim: The serum concentration of Tebipenem peaked in all routes of administration within 1 hr and then declined.
source: The serum concentration of Tebipenem peaked in all routes of administration within 1 hr and then declined, with 39 mg/kg of oral Tebipenem showing the lowest concentration in the blood at all time points (up to 6 hr) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacokinetic data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: The systemic concentration of active drug was equivalent between the 39 mg/kg of Tebipenem subcutaneously dosing and the 50 mg/kg of Tebipenem pivoxil given orally over the course of the 6-hr experiment.
source: However, the systemic concentration of active drug was equivalent between the 39 mg/kg of Tebipenem subcutaneously dosing and the 50 mg/kg of Tebipenem pivoxil given orally over the course of the 6-hr experiment (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacokinetic data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: The blood concentrations of subcutaneous Tebipenem and oral Tebipenem pivoxil were comparable, with peak concentration (Cmax) values of 71 and 62 µg/mL and systemic exposure area under the curve (AUC)0-t of 80 and 94 µg·hr/mL, respectively.
source: Notably, the blood concentrations of subcutaneous Tebipenem and oral Tebipenem pivoxil were comparable, with peak concentration (Cmax) values of 71 and 62 µg/mL and systemic exposure area under the curve (AUC)0-t of 80 and 94 µg·hr/mL, respectively (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacokinetic data presented in Table 2.

claim: The oral bioavailability of Tebipenem when dosed as Tebipenem pivoxil pro-drug was ~52%, approximately 10-fold greater in mice than oral Tebipenem as a free base (F~5%).
source: Overall, we found that the oral bioavailability of Tebipenem when dosed as Tebipenem pivoxil pro-drug was ~52%, approximately 10-fold greater in mice than oral Tebipenem as a free base (F~5%); 39 mg/kg.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacokinetic data comparing the two formulations.

claim: Two hours after an oral administration of 50 mg/kg of Tebipenem the Cmax reached a mean of 8 µg/ml in the piglets, which was equivalent to 7.5 µg/ml reported in a paediatric population.
source: Two hours after an oral administration of 50 mg/kg of Tebipenem the Cmax reached a mean of 8 µg/ml in the piglets (Figure 4B and Table 2), which was equivalent to 7.5 µg/ml reported in a paediatric population (Sato et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacokinetic data in piglets compared to published paediatric data.

claim: The AUC0-last determined in piglets was higher than AUC0-last reported in paediatric populations (32 vs 16 hr*µg/ml) but was within a comparable range.
source: The AUC0-last determined in piglets was higher than AUC0-last reported in paediatric populations (32 vs 16 hr*µg/ml, Table 2) but was within a comparable range (Sato et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacokinetic data in piglets compared to published paediatric data.

claim: High concentrations (> 300 µg/g tissue) of Tebipenem were observed in the duodenum and jejunum 15 min after administration, which declined to >400 ng/g tissue after 240 min.
source: We observed high concentrations ( > 300 µg/g tissue) of Tebipenem in the duodenum and jejunum 15 min after administration, which declined to >400 ng/g tissue after 240 min (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS quantification data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: Peak drug concentrations were reached in the ileum (15 µg/g tissue) after 30 min and in the caecum (11 µg/g tissue) and colon (6 µg/g tissue) after 60 min.
source: Peak drug concentrations were reached in the ileum (15 µg/g tissue) after 30 min and in the caecum (11 µg/g tissue) and colon (6 µg/g tissue) after 60 min.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS quantification data.

claim: The highest concentrations of the drug after 4 hr were found in the caecum.
source: The highest concentrations of the drug after 4 hr were found in the caecum (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS quantification data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: Tebipenem pivoxil could be detected in the intestinal lumen in the jejunum and the ileum, but not in the caecum and the colon at 15 min post administration.
source: The imaging from the early time point indicated that Tebipenem pivoxil could be detected in the intestinal lumen in the jejunum and the ileum, but not in the caecum and the colon (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by MALDI imaging data presented in Figure 4E.

claim: At 15 min post administration, Tebipenem free base could be detected both in the lumen and associated with enterocytes in the jejunum and the ileum.
source: At the same early time point, Tebipenem free base could be detected both in the lumen and associated with enterocytes in the jejunum and the ileum.
evidence: This is supported by MALDI imaging data.

claim: The free base appeared to be concentrated in cells lining the caecum after 15 min.
source: Notably, the free base appeared to be concentrated in cells lining the caecum after 15 min.
evidence: This is supported by MALDI imaging data.

claim: At 60 min post administration, Tebipenem free base could be detected in the lumen and enterocytes throughout the gut, whereas Tebipenem pivoxil was not detectable in the lumen.
source: At the later time point (60 min), Tebipenem free base could be detected in the lumen and enterocytes throughout the gut, whereas Tebipenem pivoxil was not detectable in the lumen (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by MALDI imaging data presented in Figure 4E.

claim: Approximately 50% of Tebipenem pivoxil is hydrolysed in the intestinal lumen, where the free drug may inhibit growth of bacteria present in the lumen.
source: These data, in combination the oral pharmacokinetics data, showing Tebipenem pivoxil has 50% (%F = 52 ± 1, Table 2) bioavailability, suggest that ~50% of Tebipenem pivoxil is hydrolysed in the intestinal lumen, where the free drug may inhibit growth of bacteria present in the lumen.
evidence: This is an inference based on the bioavailability data and MALDI imaging.

claim: 50% of the dosed Tebipenem pivoxil can penetrate the enterocytes lining the gut surface and is immediately hydrolysed.
source: Additionally, 50% of the dosed Tebipenem pivoxil can penetrate the enterocytes lining the gut surface and is immediately hydrolysed (Tebipenem pivoxil pro-drug was not detected within enterocytes by MALDI-TOF), making the drug ideal for the treatment of invasive gut bacteria.
evidence: This is an inference based on the bioavailability data and MALDI imaging showing no prodrug in enterocytes.

claim: The administration of 50 mg/kg of oral Tebipenem pivoxil resulted in a 2.3-log reduction of S. flexneri 2457T organisms in the small intestine compared to no antimicrobial 24 hours after infection.
source: Twenty-four hours after an intraperitoneal infection with 1 × 107 S. flexneri 2457T, the administration of 50 mg/kg of oral Tebipenem pivoxil resulted in a 2.3-log reduction of organisms in the small intestine compared to no antimicrobial (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo efficacy data in mice presented in Figure 5A.

claim: The quantity of S. flexneri 2457T in the small intestine in mice treated with oral Tebipenem pivoxil was significantly lower than in mice treated with 39 mg/kg of Tebipenem freebase subcutaneously (1.2-log reduction, p < 0.05).
source: The quantity of S. flexneri 2457T in the small intestine in mice treated with oral Tebipenem pivoxil was significantly lower at the same time point in mice treated with 39 mg/kg of Tebipenem freebase subcutaneously (1.2-log reduction, p < 0.05; independent t-test) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo efficacy data in mice with statistical analysis presented in Figure 5A.

claim: A comparable trend with respect to a reduction in Shigella CFUs was observed in the large intestine (p < 0.05).
source: We observed a comparable trend with respect to a reduction in Shigella CFUs in the large intestine (p < 0.05; independent t-test).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo efficacy data in mice with statistical analysis.

claim: Neither Tebipenem pivoxil nor Tebipenem freebase reduced the bacterial load in the small or large intestine to below detectable limits and did not perform as well as 40 mg/kg of oral ciprofloxacin.
source: Notably, neither formulation reduced the bacterial load in the small or large intestine to below detectable limits and did not perform as well as 40 mg/kg of oral ciprofloxacin.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo efficacy data in mice comparing different treatments.

claim: Tebipenem pivoxil significantly reduced the severity of diarrhoea and frequency of diarrheal stools in infected gnotobiotic piglets compared to control animals (p < 0.001 for AUC of score plots).
source: Tebipenem pivoxil significantly reduced the severity of diarrhoea and frequency of diarrheal stools in infected gnotobiotic piglets compared to control animals (p < 0.001 for AUC of score plots; Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo efficacy data in piglets with statistical analysis presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Tebipenem-treated piglets generally gained more weight than control vehicle-treated piglets, but this difference was not statistically significant.
source: Over the course of the 6-day experiment, Tebipenem-treated piglet generally gained more weight than control vehicle-treated piglets, but this difference was not statistically significant (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo efficacy data in piglets presented in Figure 5C.

claim: A single dose of Tebipenem pivoxil given 24 hr after infection reduced the CFU/g Shigella in stool from 1 × 107 to zero within 24 hr.
source: A single dose of Tebipenem pivoxil given 24 hr after infection reduced the CFU/g Shigella in stool from 1 × 107 to zero within 24 hr, whilst untreated animals maintained a high concentration of Shigella in their stool for the duration of the experiment (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo efficacy data in piglets presented in Figure 5D.

claim: Untreated animals maintained a high concentration of Shigella in their stool for the duration of the experiment.
source: A single dose of Tebipenem pivoxil given 24 hr after infection reduced the CFU/g Shigella in stool from 1 × 107 to zero within 24 hr, whilst untreated animals maintained a high concentration of Shigella in their stool for the duration of the experiment (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo efficacy data in piglets presented in Figure 5D.

claim: The histopathology showed a marked reduction in intestinal lesions and inflammation between the placebo-treated group and the group who received Tebipenem pivoxil.
source: The histopathology showed a marked reduction in intestinal lesions and inflammation between the placebo-treated group and the group who received Tebipenem pivoxil; with the sections showing an obvious reduction in both inflammatory cells and infecting organisms (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by histopathology data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: The sections showed an obvious reduction in both inflammatory cells and infecting organisms in Tebipenem pivoxil-treated piglets compared to placebo.
source: The histopathology showed a marked reduction in intestinal lesions and inflammation between the placebo-treated group and the group who received Tebipenem pivoxil; with the sections showing an obvious reduction in both inflammatory cells and infecting organisms (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by histopathology data presented in Figure 5E.

claim: Tebipenem pivoxil is broad spectrum.
source: Tebipenem pivoxil has many suitable characteristics for the treatment of infections caused by MDR and XDR Gram-negative bacteria; it is broad spectrum, it is rapidly bactericidal, it is already used in paediatric clinical practice (Kataoka et al., 2016), and it can be administered orally (Arends et al., 2019), making it highly suited for the treatment of gastrointestinal infections in the community.
evidence: This is supported by the MIC data against multiple bacterial species.

source: Tebipenem pivoxil has many suitable characteristics for the treatment of infections caused by MDR and XDR Gram-negative bacteria; it is broad spectrum, it is rapidly bactericidal, it is already used in paediatric clinical practice (Kataoka et al., 2016), and it can be administered orally (Arends et al., 2019), making it highly suited for the treatment of gastrointestinal infections in the community.

claim: Tebipenem exhibited high level of potency against a broad panel of >300 clinically relevant MDR enteric pathogens.
